#700. Gambit Gets Serious: Channing Tatum’s Superhero Is ‘Not All Laughs’ in ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ as Kevin Feige Promises Fans a ‘Fully-Rounded Character’

When Channing Tatum returns as Gambit in “Avengers: Doomsday,” he will be a “fully-rounded character” and not just a supporting player used for non-stop laughs and cool action scenes. That was mostly Gambit’s purpose during his Marvel Cinematic Universe debut in 2024’s “Deadpool & Wolverine.” Fans have been wondering ever since Tatum was confirmed for “Doomsday” how the MCU would navigate the tone of Gambit moving forward.

“He’s a standout,” Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige told Empire magazine about Tatum’s Gambit in the upcoming “Doomsday” movie. “It’s fun to see Gambit be as charismatic as he was in ‘Deadpool & Wolverine,’ and yet in ‘Doomsday’ it’s not all for laughs. He’s a fully-rounded character.” Related Stories Patrick Stewart's Final Movie Is 'Avengers: Doomsday'; He Said Before His Death That 'I Can’t Imagine Retiring. I’ll Forever Be an Actor' Oscar Predictions: Film Editing — ‘You Can See Everything’ Looks to Crash a Race of Past Winners and Become the Third Documentary Ever Nominated

Tatum previously revealed in a Variety cover story last year that Gambit would be softening his thick Cajun accent in “Avengers: Doomsday.” The actor spent years trying and failing to get a standalone Gambit movie made under 20th Century Fox. A running joke in “Deadpool and Wolverine” is that nobody can understand the superhero’s thick Cajun accent. Ryan Reynolds’ Deadpool quips at one point: “Who’s your dialect coach? The Minions?”

“I’m not gonna go full Cajun,” Tatum said at the time. “[Directors Anthony and Joe Russo] want things to be funny, but they don’t want to go full ‘Deadpool.’ They want to keep the drama and keep it tight. When Gambit gets serious — when he drops the Mardi Gras mask — things do matter.”

Tatum also told Variety that studio executives “really had to wrap their mind around the accent and how people are going to understand him” as Gambit moves forward in the MCU beyond “Deadpool and Wolverine.” Fans know very little of how Gambit will be utilized in “Doomsday,” although trailers have showed him facing off in battle against Simu Liu’s Shang-Chi. Tatum told Variety last year that he suffered an injury on set that resulted in him taking pain medication and undergoing intensive physical therapy. He had to be sidelined from some action scenes due to the injury, instead sitting in for close-ups of his face while relying on his stunt double to do the heavy lifting.

“Avengers: Doomsday” is set for release on Dec. 18 from Disney and Marvel Studios.

Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap.

SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on an unprecedented mission today (Nov. 13), and you can watch the action live.

Starship is scheduled to launch on its 15th test flight today from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). SpaceX plans to bring both of Starship's stages back to Starbase for a catch by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — something it has never done before.

You can watch it all live here at Space.com. And there should be a lot to see: Starship Flight 15 will last more than 22 hours, if all goes according to plan.

Starship consists of two elements: a huge booster known as Super Heavy and an upper-stage spacecraft called Starship, or Ship for short. Both are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first in the world of orbital spaceflight.

The rapidity of Starship's reuse hinges heavily on SpaceX's recovery strategy: Returning both vehicles directly to the launch mount will enable much faster inspection, refurbishment and reflight, the company has said.

SpaceX has already caught Super Heavy, pulling the feat off on three previous Starship test flights. But it has never tried to do so with Ship, which flies farther and faster than the booster and is therefore a more challenging vehicle to recover.

So today's flight is a pretty big deal for SpaceX.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," the company wrote in a Flight 15 mission description.

The action will unspool over two days, if all goes to plan. Super Heavy will return to Starbase for a touchdown just 6.5 minutes after launch, but Ship will continue on to low Earth orbit.

The upper stage will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites, during a 42-minute stretch beginning about 35 minutes after liftoff. This will be just the second batch of V3 spacecraft to reach orbit, after the 26 that went up on Flight 14 on Sept. 28.

Ship will then stay aloft for nearly a full day. The mission plan calls for the upper stage to return to Starbase for its chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), about 22.5 hours after liftoff.

There's no guarantee things will go according to plan, however. SpaceX will call off a Ship catch if the vehicle experiences any issues during Flight 15. If something crops up, the company will steer Ship to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, either near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.

So it'll be a busy weekend for SpaceX, and for space fans who want to keep tabs on the mission. And we can help you out there, with our Flight 15 updates page.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. #698. Scientists uncover a 192-year-old mystery hidden in a mangled silver coin

A badly distorted British silver coin dating to 1834 may hold evidence of an unusual accident during the minting process nearly 200 years ago. New scientific analysis suggests that the remarkable damage to the coin was more likely caused by a manufacturing problem than by ordinary wear, corrosion, or a later impact.

The findings, reported by IA STUDIO in the journal npj Heritage Science, center on a silver sixpence issued during the reign of King William IV. The coin was found in an album containing various coins at a car boot sale in Greater Manchester, England. Although the sixpence had an individual price tag of £8, the entire album was subsequently purchased as a single lot rather than the coin being bought separately.

What makes this particular sixpence remarkable is the extent and unusual pattern of its damage. Its central surface appears severely crushed and distorted, yet much of the outer rim and the small grooves along its edge remain relatively intact. The contrast raised an intriguing question about what could have happened to the coin.

To investigate, researchers examined the silver piece using powerful microscopes, chemical testing, and detailed three-dimensional surface measurements. The results point toward an unusual sequence of intense compression, potentially while the coin was being struck at the mint.

A Crushed Silver Coin Reveals Unusual Clues

The most striking evidence came from the coin's severely distorted central regions. Detailed measurements revealed deep, sharply defined depressions, elevated ridges, stepped surfaces, and areas where the metal appeared to have been pushed and displaced in overlapping patterns.

These features were particularly pronounced on the front of the coin, known as the obverse, which bears the portrait of William IV. Across the damaged central portrait area, the difference between the highest and lowest measured points reached approximately 0.75 millimeters.

That may sound small, but it represents a substantial distortion on the surface of a thin silver coin.

The investigators found that the overall damage was most consistent with repeated applications of high pressure concentrated in a limited area. The metal also appears to have been at least partly prevented from spreading outward as the force was applied.

This combination of heavy central damage and relatively well-preserved edges is difficult to reconcile with the gradual effects of circulation or simple corrosion. It also makes a single later impact, with the metal free to move outward, a less convincing explanation.

Instead, the findings favor an unusual problem during the original striking process, although the available evidence does not establish the exact sequence of events with certainty.

Microscopic Analysis Reveals Damage Beneath the Surface

To better understand the unusual deformation, the investigation combined scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX) and optical surface profilometry.

The microscopic and chemical examinations provided information about the coin's metal composition and the changes affecting its surface.

In areas that had escaped the worst damage, testing identified an underlying silver and copper alloy. The more severely distorted regions contained lower measured concentrations of silver, higher levels of copper, and additional chemical evidence associated with corrosion and contamination.

These substances were especially concentrated inside the depressions formed by the damaged metal.

However, the chemical results largely reflected changes at the surface. Although corrosion and contamination had affected the coin, they could not adequately account for the depth, shape, and distribution of its unusual distortions.

The team also used optical surface profilometry, a technique that maps the height and shape of a surface in three dimensions. This made it possible to examine the coin's damaged areas in much greater detail than ordinary photographs could provide.

The resulting maps showed steep depressions, raised shoulders, abrupt changes in surface height, and multiple layers of metal displacement.

Using height measurements supplied by the Oxford Materials Characterisation Service, the study's author determined that the damaged central portrait region varied in height by approximately 750 micrometers, equivalent to 0.75 millimeters.

Taken together, the findings suggest that the coin underwent repeated compression while its sideways movement was at least partly restricted. This explanation fits the evidence better than ordinary wear, which generally smooths a coin's surface over time, or corrosion, which tends to remove or chemically alter material.

A Rare Glimpse Into 19th-Century Coin Production

The sixpence was produced in 1834, when Britain was already using steam-powered presses to manufacture coins.

During this period, coins with serious striking defects were typically identified through mint inspections and melted down so the metal could be reused. This was especially important for coins made from precious metals such as silver.

If the unusual deformation occurred during the original minting process, the sixpence may therefore represent a rare surviving example of a manufacturing failure that would ordinarily have been removed from circulation before it ever reached the public.

Such a coin could provide a physical record of a brief mechanical problem during the early era of mechanized coin production.

Determining whether the damage actually occurred at the mint is challenging, however. Historic metal objects can undergo many changes over decades or centuries, and severe deformation may obscure the physical clues needed to identify its origin.

To address this uncertainty, the study examined several kinds of evidence independently. The researchers considered the composition of the underlying metal, chemical changes at the surface, and the three-dimensional geometry of the deformation before comparing the results with different possible explanations.

The findings also demonstrate how non-destructive scientific techniques can be used to investigate other historic metal objects. By combining chemical and structural evidence, researchers may be able to distinguish manufacturing defects from later damage even when visual inspection alone provides no clear answer.

How AI Helped Investigate the Coin Mystery

The investigation also explored how computational tools, including artificial intelligence, could assist in evaluating a historical mystery without replacing physical scientific evidence.

Before any laboratory results were available, the author began by studying high-resolution photographs of the sixpence and systematically reviewing its unusual surface features.

This early examination helped identify several possible causes of the damage and establish what kinds of physical measurements would be needed to test them.

Human-supervised computational tools, including large language models (LLMs), helped organize the observations, develop alternative explanations, compare competing ideas, and formulate questions that could later be investigated through laboratory testing.

Importantly, the initial hypotheses and analytical notes were recorded before the independently produced laboratory measurements became available.

The possible explanations included ordinary circulation wear and corrosion, mechanical damage occurring after minting, later compression under restricted conditions, and deformation during the original manufacturing process.

To investigate these possibilities, independent measurements were commissioned from the Experimental Techniques Centre at Brunel University of London and the Oxford Materials Characterisation Service within the Department of Materials at the University of Oxford.

Once the testing was completed, computational tools were used again to help organize the resulting data and compare the physical findings with the earlier explanations.

"The important sequence was hypothesis first, independent laboratory measurement second," said A. Ikraam, founder of IA STUDIO and author of the study.

"We used the models to ask what features mattered and what evidence could distinguish one explanation from another. Then the laboratory measurements gave us something physical to test those ideas against. The models could support the reasoning process, but they could not decide what happened to the coin."

Scientific Evidence Points to a Possible Minting Error

Although artificial intelligence played a supporting role in organizing observations and evaluating competing possibilities, it did not produce the laboratory measurements or determine the final findings.

The study's conclusions were based on independently generated scientific data, with the author retaining responsibility for interpreting the evidence and deciding which explanation was best supported.

The results favor a rare minting anomaly involving repeated, highly concentrated pressure, rather than damage caused by ordinary circulation, corrosion, or a single unrestricted impact after production. Nevertheless, the research does not conclusively establish every detail of what happened to the sixpence.

Beyond shedding light on the possible origins of a strangely mangled 1834 coin, the investigation illustrates how modern imaging, chemical analysis, and carefully evaluated computational tools can work together to uncover clues hidden in historic objects.

What initially appeared to be little more than a badly damaged silver coin may instead preserve an unusual record of how something went wrong during the early days of mechanized coin manufacturing.

#697. Hollywood Still Faces Weekend Disruptions After FAA Lifts Flight Ground Stop

The Motion Picture Academy's Governors Awards, the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony and numerous other events could still face delays amid flight cancellations

UPDATED: In the wake of a four-hour long flight ground stop, Hollywood can still expect a weekend of disruptions after the Federal Aviation Administration lifted the shutdown Friday evening. Travel plans were thrown into question for talent, executives and buyers headed to and from Los Angeles and New York during one of the busiest stretches on the industry calendar.

The FAA says it grounded flights “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It marks the most extensive disruption to air travel in the U.S. since the federal government mandated a total shutdown of all activity after the 9/11 attacks in September 2001. Some flights resumed immediately, but hundreds of others were canceled while travelers scrambled to make new plans. SpaceX has a message for itself, and for the spacecraft set to make history today (Nov. 13): Don't panic.

The company's Starship megarocket will conduct its 15th test flight this afternoon, a landmark liftoff that will feature the first-ever attempt to catch both of its stages with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), SpaceX rolled the Flight 15 upper stage, a vehicle known as Ship 42, out to the launch pad at its Starbase site in South Texas to prep. The company shared photos of the move on X, and in two of those shots we can see some intriguing words inked on the spacecraft: "Don't panic."

The phrase is familiar to fans of Douglas Adams' sci-fi classic "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy": In the novel, the electronic guidebook that helps travelers find their way across the cosmos has "Don't panic!" on its cover.

And Ship 42 itself is connected to the beloved book, by virtue of its serial number. In "The Hitchhiker's Guide," a supercomputer named Deep Mind is asked to come up with "the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything." It thinks for 7.5 million years and comes up with "42."

SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk has voiced his affection for "The Hitchhiker's Guide" in the past — and he has already paid tribute to it with a well-placed "Don't panic."

The debut launch of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket back in February 2018 sent Musk's red Tesla Roadster into orbit around the sun, with a spacesuit-clad mannequin named Starman at the wheel and its entertainment display programmed to read "Don't panic!"

Starship Flight 15 is scheduled to launch today during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). You can watch it here at Space.com.

If all goes according to plan, Starship's Super Heavy first stage will come back to Starbase for a chopsticks catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

Ship 42, meanwhile, will head to orbit, a destination that Starship reached for the first time on Flight 14, which took place on Sept. 28. Ship 42 will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites today — the second batch of the spacecraft to reach orbit. (The first set of 26 were delivered on Flight 14).

Ship 42 will stay up for a while after that, circling Earth 14 times before coming back for its own chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after launch.

That's the plan, anyway; SpaceX will only go through with a Ship catch attempt if all systems on the vehicle look good. If there are any problems, the company will divert to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, near either Hawaii or Chile.

Both of Starship's stages — Super Heavy and the Ship — are designed to be rapidly reusable. And "rapidly" is a bit of understatement: SpaceX wants to launch 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030, Musk has said.

The chopsticks-catch strategy is a big part of that vision. Bringing both Starship stages directly back to the launch mount will greatly reduce the time needed for inspection, refurbishment and reflight, according to SpaceX.

The company has already caught Super Heavy on three previous Starship test flights. It has never tried to do so with Ship, instead targeting ocean splashdowns with the upper stage.

The double catch attempt may be unprecedented, but SpaceX seems to be taking its own advice: There's no panic around Flight 15 or its bold goals.

"I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," Musk said last month, during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call.

#694. NASA’s CHAPEA Mars crew finally emerges after more than a year in isolation

After spending more than a year experiencing what life could be like on Mars, four NASA volunteers have finally stepped outside, marking the end of an ambitious experiment designed to prepare humans for future missions to the Red Planet.

The crew completed their simulated Mars journey on October 31, 2026, emerging into the outside world for the first time in more than a year. Although the volunteers never actually left Earth, their extended mission recreated many of the challenges astronauts could encounter while living and working millions of miles from home.

The experiment was part of NASA's Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) program, which investigates how people adapt to the demanding conditions of extended space exploration.

The four volunteers were Matthew Montgomery (left), James Spicer (middle left), Ross Elder (middle right), and Ellen Ellis (right). Following the completion of their mission, the crew posed together outdoors, celebrating their return from a simulated journey to another planet.

Throughout the experiment, the participants carried out tasks similar to those that future Mars explorers may need to perform. These included operating and testing essential systems, caring for crops, conserving limited supplies, and conducting extravehicular activities.

Extravehicular activities, often called spacewalks, are operations astronauts perform outside their spacecraft or habitat. In a Mars simulation, these activities help researchers examine how crews might prepare for and carry out work beyond the safety of their living quarters.

The volunteers also had to manage communication delays, an important challenge for anyone traveling to Mars. Unlike astronauts aboard the International Space Station, who can communicate with Earth almost instantly, future Mars explorers will experience significant delays because radio signals take time to cross the enormous distance between the two planets.

These delays mean astronauts cannot always depend on immediate guidance from mission control. They must be prepared to solve problems, make decisions, and manage unexpected situations with greater independence.

One of the biggest challenges of sending people to Mars is keeping them healthy, productive, and safe during long periods away from Earth. A crew must be able to manage food, equipment, living conditions, and daily responsibilities while working together in a confined environment.

NASA uses analog missions to explore these challenges before attempting actual journeys into deep space. An analog mission is a realistic simulation that reproduces selected conditions of space exploration while allowing scientists to study how people respond in a controlled setting on Earth.

The CHAPEA program provides an opportunity to investigate how astronauts might handle the practical demands of extended missions, including resource limitations, equipment maintenance, food production, and communication difficulties.

The lessons learned from Montgomery, Spicer, Elder, and Ellis will help NASA plan future human exploration missions. Their experiences are expected to inform the development of NASA's planned Moon Base and preparations for eventual crewed expeditions to Mars.

Although this crew's journey took place entirely on Earth, the knowledge gained could help address some of the challenges humans will face when they finally travel to the Red Planet.

#693. JB Smoove Talks Creativity and Fighting AI Fears, Evan Shapiro Breaks Down the Digital Entertainment Economy at Variety’s Business Managers Breakfast

Candice Bergen presents the Business Manager of the Year kudo to Citrin Cooperman's Arnie Herrmann

JB Smoove brought his signature creative swagger and Evan Shapiro broke down the digital entertainment economy during lively conversations held as part of Variety‘s annual Business Managers Breakfast presented by City National Bank.

The event, held Thursday in West Hollywood, hosted Variety’s 2026 Business Managers Elite honorees and recognized Citrin Cooperman’s Arnie Herrmann as Business Manager of the Year. Attendees listened to a keynote conversation with actor, comedian, producer and writer Smoove, as well as a presentation from media analyst Evan Shapiro. Related Stories Gambit Gets Serious: Channing Tatum's Superhero Is 'Not All Laughs' in 'Avengers: Doomsday' as Kevin Feige Promises Fans a 'Fully-Rounded Character' Florence Pugh Says 'I'm Not Standing for Bulls--- Behavior' on Set Anymore: 'Show Up on Time, Don’t Be Rude, Don’t Be a Misogynist'

Read below for key takeaways from the breakfast:

City National Bank president and CEO Howard Hammond kicked off the morning.

“You’re a core part of the past of City National Bank,” he told the SRO crowd of business managers. “But more importantly, our future will always be intertwined with entertainment and sports.”

He thanked attendees for their support as clients and “blunt feedback,” and recalled a conversation where Arnie Herrmann said the two things that made his career what it is today were trust and service.

The actor, comedian and entrepreneur sat down with Variety executive editor for television Michael Schneider, where he emphasized the importance of taking control.

“I do believe you have to start early and think about where you’re going to end up at. But be open to changing yourself as you go along,” Smoove said. If you don’t, “you are basically in a mental zombie apocalypse” trying to catch up when you finally get hungry for success.

Smoove said he himself has been at least five different people in his lifetime, and credits his comedic senses and thick skin for that flexibility and resilience. “Everything I ever wanted to do, I’m taking a swing in,” he said.

Still, he doesn’t limit himself to only being a comedian. Smoove was a finalist to join the cast of “Saturday Night Live,” but was eventually hired as a writer. It wasn’t something he had done before, but “sometimes you gotta play the long ball for later,” he said. “You prepare for that moment, and I’m great in the moment.”

LISTEN to highlights from the JB Smoove and Evan Shapiro conversations on Variety‘s “Strictly Business” podcast

The comedian tells people all the time to take an improv class. “You’ll be surprised how that’s going to come in handy when you’re selling real estate, or you’re building a company or you’re a small business owner,” Smoove said. “It helps being able to change gears in the moment.”

Smoove launched comedy-focused creative advertising agency The First Darrin in 2025 with United Entertainment Group CEO Jarrod Moses. With that company, he focuses on creating memorable and daring campaigns.

He also formed Alternate Side Productions and has several projects in the works under that banner. “You got to almost constantly sell yourself, and there’s nothing wrong with that,” Smoove said. “I think I’m a great salesman, and when I show up, it’s always 200%.”

Smoove credits his successes — like appearing on “Curb Your Enthusiasm” or in two Spider-Man films — to, again, driving his own vehicle. “You gotta make chess moves,” he said.

With his production company and ad agency, Smoove shows his creativity. “If you’re scared of AI, you ain’t shit,” he said. “If you are worried about something that’s coming in, you don’t have faith in the human mind.”

Evan Shapiro spoke with Cynthia Littleton, Variety co-Editor in Chief, about his take on the “affinity economy” and its impact on the entertainment industry.

Shapiro calls it the affinity economy, rather than the attention economy. He sees the companies that are successful have a creator mindset and serve the entire consumer.

“Most content does want to be free,” Shapiro said. His research shows that YouTube is at the top for total attention, which he credits to the fact that is free.

Ultimately, though, any major business will be “detrimental” to artists. “It’s not a corporation,” Shapiro said. “It’s not a foundation. It’s not a museum. It’s not a charity. They’re in it to make money.”

One of 2026’s biggest box office successes came in the form of “Obsession,” from YouTuber Curry Barker. “This guy is the new Tarantino,” Shapiro said. “It’s not because he has a massive following. It’s because he knows how to engage fans today.”

The quality of fan engagement and ability to manage that community is essential for artists today. “There’s a reason why The Rock can’t open a movie on his own without Kevin Hart,” Shapiro pointed out.

The box office may seem like it has recovered, Shapiro said, but that is because the ticket price has increased 128% this century. Will there ever be “Seinfeld” and “Friends” level syndication profits flowing in again to creatives and others in Hollywood’s creative community? Shapiro thinks so, but it will be with a different approach. “Hollywood and the traditional media ecosystem are not being disrupted,” he said. “They’re being reinvented.”

Emmy and Golden Globe Award-winning actress Candice Bergen introduced Arnie Herrmann, following two video messages from two other longtime Herrmann clients, Liam Neeson and Martin Scorsese.

“He’s intelligent, he’s modest, he has a nobility, he behaves himself,” Bergen said of Herrmann. “He’s just someone that you really would appreciate as a friend and as a guy to handle your cash.”

Longtime business manager Arnie Herrmann spoke from the heart as he accepted Variety‘s Business Manager of the Year kudo. Based in New York, Herrmann has nearly 40 of experience as a business manager and joined his current firm of Citrin Cooperman in 2010.

He recalled a colleague asking him during a brief stint at a large accounting firm, “Why keep score if we can play the game?” Herrmann took that advice to heard and left that firm to work for a boutique outfit, where he discovered his love for the business management profession.

Herrmann highlighted how lucky he feels to advise legendary entertainers, trailblazing women journalists, EGOT-winning producers, Michelin Award-winning chefs, music executives and New York City real estate pioneers. He shared a message he received from a longtime (unnamed) client when he told the client that he was nearing retirement.

“You’ve served your firm and your clients so spectacularly with such heart. Now it’s Act Three, the most important, the last one, the one where you’re meant to put everything you’ve learned in Acts One and Two and put it to work so that it’s the richest and most satisfying of all,” Herrmann read from the message. “I never like goodbyes, but it’s not. It’s farewell, and Arnie, if someone deserves farewell, it’s you. So I just wanted to say this again in a form where my voice can’t catch, because you sit up way high in our lives and liability be damned, you are much more to me than a business manager and you have been for so long.”

Herrmann also thanked his longtime clients, Variety, Citrin Cooperman colleagues, City National Bank and his family.

“The Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl famously once said, ‘He who has a why can bear almost any how,’” Herrmann said. “Now he said this under dire circumstances, but in a much lighter scenario, I can apply it here. If the ‘how’ are the long hours, the missed family time, the missed events, the ‘why’ is my love for you, my family.”

#691. 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian

A remarkable fossil discovery in China has revealed an ancient amphibian that lived entirely in the ocean, something no amphibian alive today is known to do. The unusual animal, named Gerrothorax maritimus, had a broad, flattened body protected by bony armor and was roughly the size of a giant salamander. Researchers believe it spent much of its life on the seafloor, waiting to ambush passing prey.

The discovery comes from an international team at the University of California, Davis, Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. Their findings, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, are based on two exceptionally well-preserved skeletons dating back nearly 237 million years to the Late Triassic period.

Both fossils were uncovered in China's Guizhou Province, in a region that was once submerged beneath an ancient ocean hundreds of miles from major landmasses.

"This area is part of an ecosystem that we've been looking at and trying to reconstruct," said study corresponding author Ryosuke Motani, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at UC Davis. "We've been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian, and it's a sort of very unusual member of the lineage."

The finding is especially surprising because amphibians are generally unable to survive in seawater. Among the more than 8,000 amphibian species living today, none are known to spend their entire lives in marine environments, and fewer than 2% have any ability to tolerate salt.

Mammals, reptiles, and birds, by comparison, all include species that can live entirely at sea without relying on land for food or fresh water. Until this discovery, scientists had never identified convincing fossil evidence of an amphibian with the same ability.

A Giant Armored Amphibian Built for the Seafloor

Because the two skeletons are so complete, researchers were able to piece together the animal's appearance and develop a clearer picture of how it lived.

Gerrothorax maritimus measured nearly three feet long, but its proportions were far different from those of a modern salamander. Rather than having a long, slender body, it was unusually broad and flattened, with a distinctive disc-shaped form.

Its body was also covered in thick bony armor, which may have helped protect it from large marine predators such as ichthyosaurs.

"If you think about today's amphibians, this animal is unusual because it's big," Motani said. "It's probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what's different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky."

The structure of its skull, together with its heavy armor, suggests that this ancient amphibian was an ambush predator. Instead of actively chasing its meals, it likely rested on the seafloor until an unsuspecting animal came within reach.

"They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in," said Motani, who noted that the hunting strategy resembles that of the wobbegong, a type of carpet shark that lives near the seafloor and captures prey using suction.

How Could an Amphibian Survive in Salt Water?

One of the biggest mysteries surrounding Gerrothorax maritimus is how it managed to survive in an environment that is hostile to nearly all modern amphibians.

The problem comes down largely to amphibian skin. Unlike the relatively waterproof skin of many other animals, amphibian skin allows water and gases to pass through it. This makes it useful for breathing and maintaining hydration, but also leaves amphibians especially vulnerable to the effects of salt water.

"That skin is permeable, and that allows the animals to use it for multiple purposes," said Motani. "They use it for respiration and water intake, so amphibians don't drink or breathe through the mouth because they can do both through the skin."

As a result, modern amphibians generally depend on freshwater habitats or environments close to them. A few species have developed limited salt tolerance, including the crab-eating frog. Even these animals can lose weight when exposed to brackish water and must eventually return to freshwater to recover.

The ancient Gerrothorax maritimus, however, may have evolved a very different solution.

Researchers suggest that its extensive bony armor restricted the movement of water through its skin. This protective covering may have reduced its dependence on absorbing water directly through the skin, allowing the animal to take in seawater through its mouth instead.

Under this proposed mechanism, water would have been absorbed through the digestive tract, while the animal's gills could have helped eliminate excess salt. Gills are known to have been present in members of the Gerrothorax genus, giving the researchers reason to suspect that this species possessed a more fishlike approach to managing its salt balance.

Together, these adaptations may explain how an amphibian managed to occupy an ecological niche that remains inaccessible to its modern relatives.

Fossil Evidence Points to a Fully Marine Lifestyle

The researchers also examined whether Gerrothorax maritimus truly lived in the ocean or whether its remains might have been transported there after death.

Several clues strongly favor a marine lifestyle.

First, the skeletons were recovered from sediments deposited in a deep marine environment. Their remarkable completeness also provides important evidence about where the animals died.

"Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom," said Motani. "But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived."

The preservation of such delicate skeletal structures suggests that the bodies were not carried long distances before reaching the seafloor.

To investigate further, the team analyzed the fossils' chemical composition, focusing on the relative abundance of different forms of strontium, known as isotopes.

The results closely matched the strontium isotope signatures expected in ocean water during the Late Triassic, providing another independent line of evidence that the animals inhabited a marine environment.

Taken together, the fossil preservation, geological setting, and chemical findings make a compelling case that Gerrothorax maritimus spent its life entirely at sea.

The discovery reveals an unexpected evolutionary path for amphibians, showing that at least one ancient species appears to have overcome the biological limitations that keep its living relatives largely confined to freshwater environments.

The research received funding from the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

Materials provided by University of California - Davis. Original written by Greg Watry. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Update: United Launch Alliance has delayed the launch of its Vulcan Centaur rocket to Saturday (Nov. 14) at 12:32 p.m. ET (1732 GMT) due to a power issue in a liquid gaseous nitrogen factory that pumps propellant into the rocket. "The vehicle and spacecraft are healthy," ULA wrote in an update on X.

United Launch Alliance's (ULA) Vulcan Centaur rocket will fly on Saturday (Nov. 14) for the first time in nine months, and you can watch the action live.

A Vulcan Centaur topped with 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites is scheduled to lift off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Nov. 14 at 12:32 p.m. ET (1732 GMT).

You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of ULA, or directly via the company. Coverage will start 20 minutes before liftoff.

Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which has just a half-dozen launches left on its manifest.

Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and has flown three more times since. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024, and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs).

In both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both launches, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addresses the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.)

ULA has been working hard on that front, and the company is confident that Vulcan is ready to return to flight.

"The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update.

"To support our customers, this upcoming launch will utilize the improved nozzle design, and additional testing and analysis will continue in parallel with the mission," ULA added. "By flying the improved design, ULA gains valuable flight data that validates these improvements and is the most beneficial path in support of all our customers."

Saturday's launch will help build out Amazon's broadband constellation in low Earth orbit (LEO), which was previously called Project Kuiper but is now known as Amazon Leo. It will eventually compete with SpaceX's Starlink network, which has been up and running for several years.

Amazon Leo will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. About 400 of them have reached space to date on 15 launches, which have been conducted by three different rockets — the Atlas V, SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. Today's launch will be the first such mission for the Vulcan Centaur, which explains ULA's name for the launch — Vulcan Leo 1.

If all goes according to plan Saturday, Vulcan Centaur will deploy the 40 Amazon Leo satellites over a 25-minute span beginning about 70 minutes after launch. They'll be released roughly 270 miles (435 kilometers) above our planet.

The Amazon Leo launch could be part of a very busy 12-hour stretch. SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on Friday (Nov. 13), on a test mission that will feature the first-ever catch attempt of the vehicle's Ship upper stage. And Rocket Lab is scheduled to launch its 100th-ever mission at 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT) on Saturday (Nov. 14).

You can watch all of this action live here at Space.com when the time comes.

#689. Seth Rogen on ‘The Invite,’ ‘Tangles,’ ‘The Studio’ Season 2, Reviving ‘Darkwing Duck’ and Why ‘Any A–hole Can Write That Joke’ Was the Best Advice He Ever Got

Awards Circuit Podcast: The roundtable discusses the 'I Play Rocky' screenplay debate and the new Disney movie 'Hexed'

For years, people have told me that Seth Rogen and I are voice twins.

Sitting across from him at the Middleburg Film Festival, deep in Virginia horse country, even Jeremy, the person recording our conversation, can confirm that the resemblance is very close. Even so, the year Rogen is having belongs entirely to him.

Coming off the historic Emmy run of “The Studio,” Rogen could have gone anywhere next. He chose to travel into the world of darkly comic relationship drama “The Invite” and the 2D animated world of Alzheimer’s disease with “Tangles,” a one-two punch nobody could have seen coming. Related Stories Patrick Stewart's Final Movie Is 'Avengers: Doomsday'; He Said Before His Death That 'I Can’t Imagine Retiring. I’ll Forever Be an Actor' Oscar Predictions: Film Editing — ‘You Can See Everything’ Looks to Crash a Race of Past Winners and Become the Third Documentary Ever Nominated

In “The Invite,” Olivia Wilde’s A24 dinner-party indie, Rogen plays Joe, a husband whose fraying marriage gets stress-tested over one excruciating evening with the upstairs neighbors, played by Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton. I think it’s his finest hour as an actor. On paper, it sounds like a “another Seth Rogen” role. On screen, he plays it in a way we didn’t expect and he credits Wilde for taking his and Norton’s ideas to heart.

“She could have just not used any of it,” he says. “and I just would not have been as funny in it.”

On the episode of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast, Rogen discusses his one-two punch of “The Invite” and “Tangles,” along with the recently announced “Darkwing Duck” revival at Disney+, the awards-season satire threaded through Season 2 of “The Studio” and how “Steve Jobs” opened a door to a part of the industry he had never been invited into. Listen below!

Among comedians, he says, going dramatic “almost feels like a bit of a cheat code” and he recalls Jonah Hill predicting “Moneyball” (2011) would bring him the most acclaim of his career for doing the least (Hill was right, getting his first Oscar nom for supporting actor).

“Tangles,” on the other hand, is a different kind of gamble. The hand-drawn, black-and-white animated feature, adapted from Sarah Leavitt’s graphic memoir about her mother’s Alzheimer’s and directed by first-time feature filmmaker Leah Nelson, comes from Rogen’s Point Grey Pictures and features his voice alongside Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Abbi Jacobson, Bryan Cranston and Samira Wiley. In a category ruled by studio franchises, it is the outlier and it took 10 years to make and the Canadian multihyphenate always had his eye on what’s most important. “When we give up on it is when it doesn’t happen,” he says.

Independent Film Company and Sapan Studio open “Tangles” in theaters this year for an awards-qualifying run, with a wider expansion in early 2027. “The Invite” is streaming on HBO Max.

The conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

You’re having quite a year, with two very different movies in “The Invite” and “Tangles.” You’re coming off “The Studio,” and there’s been a lot of anticipation about what you’ll do next. This is quite a one-two punch. How does this moment in your career feel?

I feel very lucky. You only want to hope that you’re learning more in life, that you’re getting better at making choices and that once you’ve decided to do something, you get better at being the best part of the team you can be. It’s incredibly nice and gratifying that, over the last few years, I feel like I’ve been doing work I’m very proud of and pushing myself to do things that are hopefully different from what I’ve done in the past. But I also feel very lucky to have people who have wanted to work with me and have been willing to. And part of it is coincidence. We’ve worked on “Tangles” for 10 years. We didn’t know it was going to come out now. Luck has a lot to do with these things coming to life in a way that makes it seem like I planned it.

Starting with “The Invite,” this might be your finest hour as an actor. On paper, it sounds like a movie Seth Rogen would make. Playing Joe, did you feel you were doing something you hadn’t done before? Did you have one of those out-of-body experiences?

As we were making the movie, I felt like I was being given the opportunity, at least in a movie, to do something that was very representative of my exact comedic, tonal and dramatic taste. What was really amazing about what Olivia did was that she allowed us to affect the tone of the film with our performances. She allowed me to insert humor in moments where it wasn’t originally going to be, which changes the tone of the whole thing. She allowed Edward to give dramatic monologues in places where they weren’t originally going to be. And then she allowed me to make jokes that subverted those moments in ways that weren’t originally scripted.

To me, that was an incredibly new and gratifying feeling. We weren’t just being invited to change the dialogue or our characters throughout the performing process. Olivia was allowing us to change the tone of the film itself with our performances. You could see it happening in real time. You could see that a scene was much funnier than we thought it would be. Or we thought a scene was going to be funny, but it was actually much more intense than we all thought. We were encouraged to play with that and not be too beholden to what it was originally conceived as, but instead feel it out as we were doing it.

I have to give her credit for using my stuff in a way that turned out very well. I throw a lot of stuff out there, and she could have edited this movie in a way that left out some of what I think are the funniest moments I generated as we were making it. The film probably still would have been very good, but I just wouldn’t have been as funny in it.

So I’m very proud that it’s a performance people seem to like, and I genuinely feel it’s one of my funnier performances. I’ve done dramatic work in the past, and I think among comedians it almost feels like a bit of a cheat code. If I’m not funny, everyone leans in a little bit more. I remember Jonah Hill was making “Moneyball,” and he said, “This is going to be the thing that I get the most acclaim for. And it’s for sure the easiest thing I’ve done, because I’m just doing less than I normally do.” And I’ve done things like that. So what’s nice is that I do feel like I was creating comedy throughout this film, and people are appreciating that. It isn’t just because it’s not funny that people are appreciating it, which is something I think a lot of comedians have experienced.

It’s the Jim Carrey cheat code. He gets to do “The Truman Show” and “Eternal Sunshine,” and suddenly we’re all saying, “My God.”

Yes. There was a time when comedians really pursued that and wanted that, and I think it was a very deliberate thing comedians were doing for a while. I totally get it. It’s totally legitimate. It’s just that, to me, I’m very proud of my ability to generate comedy on camera. I’ve always been most proud of my funny work. It’s obviously an honor to get to be in Steven Spielberg movies and things like that are certainly less comedic, and the fact that those filmmakers think I can serve their work in any way is very flattering. But I’m always thinking, if I could also bring my full ability to make this comedic, that would be great. That’s exactly what Olivia really encouraged me to do. So it was very gratifying to be able to bring that.

I love that comedic actors can make that transition so seamlessly. I’m also dying for directors who are known for drama to go the other way. I want to see the Christopher Nolan version of “Superbad.” I want them to take a swing like that.

Apparently, “Digger” is that. I haven’t seen it yet. It’s harder than it looks sometimes. It does go both ways. Comedians try to do drama, and sometimes it’s ill-fitting. Dramatic actors try to do comedy, and sometimes that’s ill-fitting, too. I’m not saying that film is that. I haven’t seen it. But it’s something I’ve seen happen.

Then there’s “Tangles,” which is about as far from “The Invite” as you can get. The animated feature category at the Oscars has been dominated by studio franchises for years, and now we have this hand-drawn, black-and-white film about Alzheimer’s. I think people need to hear the answer to this: How difficult is it to make a movie like this?

Really hard [laughs]. We’ve been working on it for 10 years, and I think maybe the last three years of that were production. So it was about seven years of us internally developing it, but also trying to find financing, putting together a cast that would be appealing to financiers, doing readings and making sure the script was really, really good.

And the movie itself was made incredibly differently. Most animated movies, these big studio ones, are made, then made again, then made again. You screen them, redo the third act, screen them again and redo the first act. This movie couldn’t be made that way. It had to be written and then executed, and we could change almost nothing. It’s hand-drawn, so the process of changing things, should you want to, is incredibly labor-intensive and arduous.

People like Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Bryan Cranston, Samira Wiley and Abbi Jacobson, along with so many of the amazing cast members, were honestly really helpful in getting the movie made. So was having a good script and filmmakers who, when those actors got in the room with them, were willing to let them take ownership of the material. It’s so gratifying that the movie even exists. We’ve spent so long working on it.

During those first seven years, how many times did you think, “This isn’t happening?”

I thought it would happen. So many things take a long time to get made. I truly believe that if we give up on it, that’s when it doesn’t happen. Sometimes we don’t give up, and we will bring it into existence through sheer brute force. This felt worth it because it was good. If something is good, I believe you can find a way to make it. “Superbad” took so long to get made. And then there were things like “Pineapple Express” and “Sausage Party,” all these movies we worked on for so long before they were made. To me, 10 years is normal.

“Darkwing Duck” because I’m a child of the ’80s and ’90s. Congratulations on the Emmy for “The Muppet Show,” and obviously we have “The Studio” Season 2 coming. But nothing excites me more than this cartoon classic that Mark Hamill has a role in! Did that casting fall into your lap?

The cast is really great. We just cast a Scrooge McDuck who might be the most exciting casting I could ever imagine. I’ll tell you after. But it’s incredible. We’ve been working on it for a very long time. You get caught up in these corporate restructurings, but we’ve been working on “Darkwing Duck” for years and years. I’ve been watching the episodes, and they’re amazing. They’re coming together so well, and the animation is beautiful and really inventive.

I was actually surprised you didn’t go the movie route.

I’m glad we didn’t. The TV nature of it was very appealing to us, honestly. As nice as it is to make a hand-drawn, black-and-white animated film, it’s also nice to extract every penny Disney’s willing to put into a thing. Getting to work in both those ways is nice. But with something like “Darkwing Duck,” we felt that if we were going to do it, it had to be top, top-notch.

Are there other Disney shows from the ’80s and ’90s you’d love to bring back? I think of “TaleSpin,” “Gummi Bears” and “DuckTales.”

I always think of “Flight of the Navigator.” That was a Disney movie, I guess. I would never presume I’d do it, but that’s always been a movie I thought was cool. “Darkwing Duck,” though, I loved. And it’s very meta. It’s funny, I reread those “Calvin and Hobbes” comics recently and I realized they really formed a lot of my personality. Years ago, when we were first talking about doing “Darkwing Duck” again, I rewatched all of it and thought, this is really meta. It really breaks the fourth wall and comments on these shows I was also watching at the same time, at the same age.

If we can get “Gargoyles” back up and running …

That would be great. I did love “Gargoyles.”

Let’s talk about “The Studio” Season 2. There have been a lot of reports from the set: Madonna, the Venice Film Festival. Which real-life awards-season humiliation of yours is going to end up on the show?

How much does Variety figure into the new season?

I think it comes up. I don’t want to reveal too much, but some of the stuff has made it out publicly into the world a little bit. This idea of playing the awards game as a studio is definitely a theme explored throughout the season.

Do you have a Season 2 equivalent of the Martin Scorsese moment, when viewers see who’s appearing and think, “I can’t believe they got him?” Does Christopher Nolan show up, for example?

We have several of those. Some are really unbelievable, and having to direct these people has been among the most terrifying moments of my entire life. For ourselves, we really tried to be even more ambitious. We wanted to get people we were even bigger fans of and make them even bigger parts of the episodes, if we could. We also wanted to dig deeper into our own feelings about the industry and our own internal conflicts as we go about all this.

Does the awards race feel more or less relevant to you now? Having made “The Studio,” how does it look compared with 15 years ago?

What’s interesting is that until I did the “Steve Jobs” movie, which was pretty deep into my career, I was never part of anything that was on that journey in any capacity. I’d been to TIFF and South by Southwest to premiere things. But that was the first time I went to Telluride, and then we were in the New York Film Festival. Honestly, it was like a door to a secret part of the industry that I’d never been invited into was suddenly opened. So it’s interesting, because I had a very lovely career before any of this was even on my radar.

But that being said, the fact that “The Studio” won awards got us things in the second season that we probably wouldn’t have gotten in the first season. So there is some tangible outcome to some of this stuff. I understand why people get invested in it, and I understand the lure and the draw. I’ve seen people go on this journey and get the exact outcome they were hoping for, and it ultimately gave them none of the things they hoped it would. And I’ve seen people go on the journey and not get the outcome they wanted, and they had a good time and seemed to have good perspective at the end of all of it. It is a fascinating part of our industry to me.

I think especially for smaller things, it is incredibly helpful. It could make or break people’s careers. It could make or break a film. It could change the course of people’s lives. If you’ve already made many billion-dollar movies, winning best picture is a feather in your cap. It’s not going to change the course of your life, per se. But what’s interesting is those people are at these events right next to the people whose lives it will change. To me, that is really interesting to see in real life and really cool. For some people, they’re at the point of their career where awards have very personal stakes, but there are many other people here for whom the awards have real-life stakes. Will they get to do the thing they’ve always wanted to do, or will it not happen the way they hoped?

That is really interesting and scary and cool to see play out. There are those moments where your heart is pounding and you’re like, we’re doing it. This is what we asked for: to put ourselves out there and subject ourselves to reality in terms of how our work is being perceived. It can be very gratifying and incredibly scary and stressful.

Can you tell me something about “The Studio” Season 2? Is there a oner episode again?

We actually try to do much more of that. There are more episodes in a much more condensed timeline. I think there are technically several episodes this season that have no cuts in them, basically, throughout the entire thing. They’re real-time, half-hour moments in time that the episode is chronicling.

It’s a weird time in the industry. Depending on who you ask, the future looks very grim. Others say it’s an evolution and we’re just going through some changes. One of the biggest conversations here at Middleburg was Peter Rice going to Netflix. Someone like him, who’s been such a theatrical guy, making that move feels like a signal: Theatrical’s back! How do you feel about this moment? Do you get nervous, or do you think we’re going to be OK?

It’s a mixture of everything. It is everything at once. I’m very optimistic about some things. The fact that so many people are going to theaters, compared to the last few years, is so encouraging. I think we are finally getting over that hump of the pandemic and the strikes and all that. It seems like things are returning to a time when there are a lot of good movies and people are willing to go see them, and that’s really exciting. From my own personal lens, I can go to the theater on a Tuesday night and it’s packed and it wasn’t like that for a long time. As someone who loves going to the movies, it’s really fun to see. It reminds me of when I was a kid, honestly, a little bit more. And I think other things are terrifying.

“Sethical.” Friends from growing up still call me that when I see them. They don’t even think about it. It just comes out.

Something you loved as a kid but can’t believe you were into when you think about it now?

I get why people like “Magic: The Gathering,” but I spent every penny I had on “Magic: The Gathering” cards. That’s the thing I look back on, and I’m like, I should have bought other stuff.

I don’t karaoke as a rule. If karaoke went away altogether, I’d never need to be in a room with some drunk person screaming a song ever again. The rooms are getting smaller and smaller. Now I’m three feet away from this person. It used to be the bar was higher because you were subjecting yourself to a real big room full of people. Now you’re in a little room with just your friends in it, screaming your ass off like an idiot. It’s so loud. I hate it. That said, “All for Love” by Bryan Adams. If you have two other raspy-voiced friends, it’s a really good song.

I was going to say “The Apartment.” I would take “The Apartment.”

I’m pretty flexible. I can almost get my leg behind my head.

I just like vanilla. I did that movie with Barbra Streisand [”The Guilt Trip”], and she was obsessed with McConnell’s ice cream, which is from Santa Barbara. Every scene we shot, she’s like, “Wouldn’t we be eating ice cream in this scene?” So yes, it’s become McConnell’s.

My glasses come to mind. My shoes. Things like that.

What TV show or film in all of history do you wish you were a cast member of?

Maybe it would have been cool to be in “Ghostbusters” or something like that.

Which fictional character do you most relate to or admire?

I always liked Homer Simpson. Not that I relate to or admire him, but I always just liked him.

Your favorite piece of advice, either given or received?

I was told at a very young age to write what only I could write, which meant writing things based on my own experience, things that were happening to me. A stand-up comedian named Darryl Lenox, who’s passed away, unfortunately, told me that and he was really nice to me. I was writing jokes that were observational, like, “What’s the deal with crazy glue?” Those kinds of jokes. I was doing OK. I was maybe 15, maybe 14 and he pulled me aside and said, “Dude, you’re out there trying to get hand jobs and trying to buy beer and trying to sneak into parties and shit. No one else can talk about that. Talk about that. Don’t talk about fucking crazy glue. Any asshole can write that joke.” It was honestly the best creative advice I’ve ever gotten. I try to adhere to it to this day.

#688. NASA’s Parker Solar Probe discovers a hidden pattern in the Sun’s chaotic magnetic fields

Turbulence is all around us, from milk swirling into a cup of coffee to powerful storms churning through the atmosphere and oceans. But turbulence also occurs throughout space, where it behaves in ways that scientists are still struggling to understand.

Unlike the air and water on Earth, much of the matter in space consists of electrically charged particles in a state (known as the plasma state). These particles interact strongly with magnetic and electric fields, creating turbulence that is fundamentally different from what we experience on Earth. Space plasma is also so thinly spread that particles rarely collide with one another, making its behavior even more unusual.

Scientists have long struggled to explain how turbulence develops under these conditions and how energy is distributed among its constantly changing fluctuations. Now, an international research team has uncovered a surprising clue: hidden within the seemingly random motion of space plasma is a distinct magnetic pattern that reverses direction at very small scales.

The discovery, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, reveals a previously unobserved phenomenon that could improve our understanding of the solar wind and the turbulent conditions that influence space weather.

NASA's Parker Solar Probe Reveals a Hidden Magnetic Reversal

Researchers from the Technische Universität Braunschweig and the University of Tokyo, working with Tohoku University, Kyushu University, Osaka University, and other international institutions, identified the phenomenon using observations from NASA's Parker Solar Probe.

The collaboration brought together scientists from ten countries, including researchers at the Institute of Theoretical Physics at Technische Universität Braunschweig.

By analyzing highly precise measurements of magnetic fields and particles, the team discovered that turbulent magnetic fields reverse their direction of rotation at a particular range of wavelengths. This marks the first direct observation of such a reversal in space turbulence.

Even more surprisingly, the reversal becomes more pronounced and shifts toward longer wavelengths as the solar wind travels farther from the Sun.

The change occurs at a critical boundary where the behavior of plasma shifts from the collective movement of a flowing fluid to the dynamics of individual particles. This connection suggests that the magnetic reversal may provide an important new way to understand how turbulence operates across different physical scales.

Finding Order in the Chaos of Space Turbulence

At larger scales, plasma moves much like a fluid. Swirling structures called vortices and electromagnetic waves create increasingly complex fluctuations, producing the turbulent conditions found throughout space.

Although these movements appear random, the researchers discovered that the rotation of the magnetic fields follows a consistent pattern.

When viewed along a direction pointing outward from the Sun, magnetic fields at larger scales tend to rotate counterclockwise. At much smaller scales, however, the preferred rotation switches to clockwise.

This reversal occurs precisely where plasma stops behaving primarily like a fluid and begins exhibiting behavior governed by individual particles.

The finding is particularly striking because it reveals a clear, organized feature within a system otherwise dominated by seemingly unpredictable fluctuations.

"We see a clear structure in the spectrum, even though the turbulence represents unstructured motions," says Dr. Masatomi Iizawa (TU Braunschweig), the study's first author.

Dr. Yokoi (University. of Tokyo) emphasizes the broader importance of the discovery, stating, "The results are of great significance for both plasma physics and astrophysics."

Why the Discovery Matters for Solar Storms and Space Weather

Although the magnetic reversal occurs at extremely small scales, understanding it could have far-reaching consequences for space physics.

Plasma turbulence is a major feature of many environments throughout the universe, including Earth's magnetosphere, the solar wind, regions affected by solar eruptions, interplanetary space, and the disks of material surrounding astronomical objects known as accretion disks.

It also influences the shock waves and clouds of magnetic material that travel through interplanetary space following eruptions on the Sun.

These disturbances can play an important role in geomagnetic storms, making plasma turbulence a critical factor in efforts to predict space weather.

By showing how an organized magnetic pattern emerges as turbulent plasma transitions from fluid behavior to particle behavior, the new research provides an important piece of a longstanding physics puzzle. The findings could ultimately help scientists better understand the complex processes that govern the solar wind and improve the physical models used to forecast geomagnetic storms.

Materials provided by School of Science, The University of Tokyo. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap.

Having reached orbit for the first time with Starship last time out, SpaceX is looking to take a huge stride toward full reusability with Flight 15 — the first attempt to catch the megarocket's Ship upper stage, as the company eyes hourly launches by 2030.

SpaceX is targeting today (Nov. 13) for Starship's 15th flight, which will lift off from the company's Starbas site in South Texas. If all goes well, the mission — which you can watch here at Space.com — will end on Saturday (Nov. 14) with the first attempt at what SpaceX itself calls the "Holy Grail of rocketry": Catching both Starship's Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage chopstick-style back at the launch pad.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in its Flight 15 mission description.

The 75-minute Flight 15 launch window opens today at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), and a number of Starship firsts are planned for early in the flight. For example, while SpaceX has caught three Super Heavy boosters and reused two of them to date, the first attempt to catch a next-gen Super Heavy "V3" vehicle will come today, around 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

If the Ship upper stage gets the go-ahead for orbital insertion, it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites — designed especially for use on Starship — into low Earth orbit (LEO), starting about 35 minutes after launch. Then, 21 hours later, if "internally developed, and FAA-approved, conditions" for a return to Starbase and catch are met — including on-orbit assessment of Ship's heat shield by three of the V3 satellites — SpaceX will attempt to recover the orbital upper stage.

This landmark try will follow the first-ever Ship reentry over inhabited areas, as the vehicle will maneuver its way over sparsely populated regions of northern Mexico and southern Texas. (On previous missions, Ship has splashed down in the open ocean.) It will head back to Starbase and make a bellyflop maneuver as it descends to the site's Pad 2 before flipping itself vertical, ready for embrace of the launch tower's waiting mechanical arms.

"SpaceX will attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and Starship on the upcoming flight. If both are successful, it will mark the first time that all parts of an orbital rocket return to Earth intact," Elon Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Nov. 6. "This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary."

Half of the system is already proven. With catching and reflying boosters largely established, the next and unprecedented step is catching Ship. This is no easy task. The vehicle, returning from orbital speeds, must survive the heat of reentry, make its way precisely back to the pad put itself in position to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. The full recovery of an orbital launch system would, in the words of SpaceX, be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" and would open the "door to airplane-like cadence."

A successful catch would allow SpaceX to then work on refurbishing Ship for reflight, the next challenge of full reusability. Musk said in August in a SpaceX earnings call that the company will aim to refly the Super Heavy and Ship early next year.

SpaceX has a lot of experience with rocket reuse, as its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket pioneered the practice. But the company is eyeing another level of reflight with Starship: It's targeting roughly 10,000 launches of the megarocket per year by 2030, which works out to more than one launch per hour.

"We're aiming to reach 30+ Starship launches/day in 2030, which is ~10k annualized," Musk posted on X in August.

The company has repeated that figure to regulators. In comments filed with the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration in late October, it said that "SpaceX anticipates conducting 10,000 launches per year itself." Meanwhile, the recently signed National Space Transportation Policy aims to boost the U.S.'s capabilities to support more than 1,000 rocket launches per year by 2030.

Musk added that SpaceX's planned Starbase Louisiana site alone could support that many Starship launches. For context: SpaceX launched 165 Falcon 9 missions in 2025, and that was about half of the global total for orbital flights.

Why is SpaceX targeting this incredible increase in launch cadence? It wants to build satellite megaconstellations that dwarf anything the world has ever seen.

The company's V3 Starlink satellites are too large to fly efficiently on the Falcon 9. Each one of the next-gen spacecraft adds 1 terabit of capacity to SpaceX's broadband network, and the 26 flying on Flight 15 are equivalent to around 10 Falcon 9 launches packed with Starlink V2 Mini satellites, according to SpaceX. And the company wants to put a staggering 100,000 V3 Starlink satellites into orbit. (There are currently about 11,000 current-gen Starlink satellites in orbit, and that's by far the largest satellite network assembled to date.)

SpaceX's Starmind project blows even this figure out of the water. SpaceX wants to launch up to 1 million satellites to serve as orbital AI data centers, and it appears to be making the moves terrestrially regarding the hardware. On Nov. 10, German firm Singulus Technologies announced a contract worth more than 60 million euros for a solar cell production line for Starmind satellites, which SpaceX builds in Bastrop, Texas. Musk said the order covers equipment for 100 gigawatts of solar cells per year. In terms of orbital hardware, the project is only feasible if SpaceX can reach its targeted "airplane-like cadence."

The gap between SpaceX's vision and the situation today is vast. Starship flew four times in 2024 and five times in 2025, and Flight 15 would be its fourth launch of 2026. Musk said on the earnings call that he expects Starship to fly weekly at some point in the first half of 2027, and twice weekly or more by the end of that year. Starbase in Texas is currently authorized for 25 launches per year, and the Louisiana site is not expected to host a launch before 2029.

Even a perfect outing for Flight 15 and two clean catches will leave lots of work to do. SpaceX will then need to demonstrate reflight with Ship, after assessing the impact on its heat shield system. Then comes orbital refueling, which is a necessary step for any Starship trip beyond LEO and a requirement for SpaceX's commitment to NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. It's unclear how many tanker flights and refuelings will be needed to make a lunar mission possible, but, whatever the number, Starship will probably need to be rapidly reusable. Another step is carrying people. SpaceX has tested life support hardware on the ground in a crew cabin for the moon lander version of Starship that it is building for NASA, but no Starship has flown with such a system.

There are no guarantees for Flight 15. Ship will only be cleared for a return to Starbase and a catch attempt if it meets safety checks after reaching orbit, which itself is an achievement not to be taken for granted. Flight controllers may end up needing to bring Ship down in the Pacific Ocean or divert its reentry into the Gulf late into flight.

Musk told investors last month that success on this flight is "more likely than not." Whatever happens today and on Saturday, the measure of Starship's progress will soon shift from whether SpaceX can catch a Ship to how quickly it can launch one again.

Andrew is a freelance space journalist with a focus on reporting on China's rapidly growing space sector. He began writing for Space.com in 2019 and writes for SpaceNews, IEEE Spectrum, National Geographic, Sky & Telescope, New Scientist and others. Andrew first caught the space bug when, as a youngster, he saw Voyager images of other worlds in our solar system for the first time. Away from space, Andrew enjoys trail running in the forests of Finland. You can follow him on Twitter @AJ_FI.
